title: Speed Cameras Are Popping Up Everywhere, and Drivers Are Not Happy
summary:
Have you ever seen a speed camera? It's a machine that takes a picture of your car if you drive too fast. In Florida, these cameras are showing up in school zones. But some drivers are really annoyed.

Carlos Acosta got two tickets from these cameras. He says it's a "money grab"—a way for the government to make money, not keep kids safe. "I'm all for protecting the kids coming and going from school," he said. But his tickets were given during the middle of the day, when kids were inside learning. "So they're basically giving you a citation for going over the regular speed limit," he said.

Florida is not the only state with speed cameras. California, Hawaii, Michigan, and Minnesota also allow them. Now more than two dozen states have them. Safety experts say the cameras work because they make drivers slow down, which means fewer crashes and fewer deaths.

But some drivers and lawyers are fighting back. Ted Hollander, a lawyer, says the cameras should only be on when kids are around. "We feel like it's an illegal tax," he said. The Trump administration's Department of Transportation recently removed speed cameras from a list of proven safety measures, which made safety advocates upset.

Supporters of the cameras say they have many safeguards to make sure it's about safety, not money. Rep. Laura Friedman from California helped write the state's speed camera law. She says the goal is to calm traffic and save lives. Soon, Los Angeles will turn on its speed cameras—a big test in a city that loves fast cars.
why_it_matters: If your family drives near a school, this debate could change how speed rules are enforced in your town and how carefully adults drive where kids walk.

Laura Friedman is a California state representative, a lawmaker who helps make rules for her state.
